channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The US Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate from 3.75% to 4%, its first increase in three years, with chair Kevin Warsh citing a stronger economy, inflation that has not slowed, and a geopolitical landscape of shocks.
item.description:
Warsh set the decision against the July meeting, when the rate was left unchanged, and named three things that had changed since. He also pointed to economic strength, a surge in AI-related spending, and the gap between energy spot prices and crack spreads as forces driving long-term yields. Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave described a booming nominal economy — resilient real growth alongside rising inflation — as giving the Fed room, and argued that not tightening would risk demand-driven inflation taking hold as supply shocks fade. LiveMint calls the move a foregone conclusion given a relatively stable job market and the inflationary pressure from the ongoing Iran war, reports a further increase expected before the end of 2026, and notes that the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan have also raised rates, so that a renewed tightening cycle means a stronger dollar and firmer bond yields and a higher cost of capital. The reporting does not give the vote, places the meeting only in the previous week, gives no projected path beyond the expectation of one more move, and does not separate how much of current inflation is attributed to energy.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A first hike after three years changes the direction of the cost of capital rather than only its level, and direction is what investment cases are built on. Three major central banks reported as tightening together compounds that: the effect on customers' capital spending is broader than any single decision, and construction and durable goods are the end-markets where a higher discount rate shows up first and most visibly. Warsh's reference to the spread between energy spot prices and crack spreads connects this to the refining picture elsewhere in today's alert, since a rate decision partly driven by energy costs makes those two exposures correlated rather than independent. A stronger dollar also changes the translation of dollar-denominated input costs against European revenue. Points that may be worth considering include how a rising rate path affects customer investment in construction-linked markets, and whether currency and rate exposure are being read together or separately.

LiveMint | LiveMint | The Sydney Morning Herald

item.title: Friedrich Merz has called the renminbi undervalued by 25% to 30% and urged the EU to emulate the Plaza Accord to force an appreciation, while Ursula von der Leyen said the "China shock" is deindustrialising European industrial regions.
item.description:
The reporting describes the Plaza Accord only as a 1985 agreement the US imposed on Japan, and gives no further detail of the mechanism Merz has in mind. On the same days, China's foreign minister Wang Yi told German foreign minister Wadephul in a telephone call that China and Europe should not wage a trade war, and asked Germany to press the EU to reject protectionism, saying the two sides need to strengthen strategic communication; China Daily reports the two ministers agreeing that China-EU trade issues should be resolved through dialogue and consultation. So the German position runs in two directions at once: public pressure on the currency and deficit, and bilateral dialogue machinery with Beijing. The reporting gives no source for the 25% to 30% valuation range and no methodology. It does not give the size of the EU trade deficit with China, does not say what instruments the Commission is actually considering, and gives no Chinese response to the currency claim itself.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Currency and trade defence are different instruments with different timelines, and the language has moved to the one with the broader reach. A tariff or quota touches named product codes; an exchange-rate adjustment of the size named would change the landed cost of everything imported from China at once, including intermediates and equipment as well as finished goods. For a European producer that both competes with Chinese material and buys from Chinese suppliers, those two effects run in opposite directions and do not necessarily net out. The more immediate point is directional: a chancellor using this language and a Commission president using the word deindustrialisation indicate where European trade policy is heading, whatever instrument eventually carries it — and the reporting does not say what instrument the EU is considering. Points that may be worth considering include which input categories are sourced from China at what share, how a material appreciation would move both cost and competitive position, and whether the German-Chinese dialogue track produces anything concrete.

Hong Kong Economic Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Handelsblatt | China Daily

item.title: BMW, Ford, Volkswagen's Elli and energy firms including Eon have written to Germany's Federal Network Agency saying they fear its proposed "Mispel" rules would make bidirectional charging economically unattractive.
item.description:
Bidirectional charging lets an electric vehicle return stored electricity to a building or the grid rather than only drawing from it, turning the car into a storage asset. Loic Geipel of the German automotive association VDA set out the industry's objection, and an unnamed large German manufacturer is quoted saying it would be a defeat for industrial policy, with hundreds of millions of euros invested and the technology's ramp-up endangered at the point where the vehicles are ready. The reporting does not describe what the Mispel draft actually proposes, which is the central gap: without the mechanism it is not possible to judge the objection. It does not give the agency's rationale or any response from it, does not say what stage the proposal has reached or when it would take effect, and does not quantify the investment figure beyond "hundreds of millions" or attribute it to a named company.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Bidirectional charging sits at the junction of the vehicle and the building, and both sides of that junction are material-intensive. Both sides of that junction involve hardware assembly — vehicle power electronics, and building-side wallbox and storage installation — though the reporting describes no equipment or materials. A regulatory decision that determines whether the technology reaches volume would determine whether that hardware reaches volume with it. The wider signal is about German regulatory risk in electrification generally: manufacturers describing a grid-rule draft as a defeat for industrial policy is the same complaint appearing in a different instrument. This is a proposal drawing objections rather than a decision, and the objection comes from the parties with the investment at stake. Points that may be worth considering include what the draft proposes in substance, when the agency responds, and whether vehicle-to-grid assumptions sit in any current development programme.

Handelsblatt

item.title: The Global Timber Index shows Brazil at 59.2% and the Republic of the Congo at 50.0% as the only producer countries at or above the 50% expansion threshold, with Malaysia at 29.7% the weakest of the eight in contraction.
item.description:
The index is published by the International Tropical Timber Organization and works like a purchasing managers' index: readings above 50% indicate expansion, at 50% stability, below 50% contraction. The remaining readings are Ghana at 49.1% and Indonesia at 47.9%, described as slight contraction; Thailand at 45.6%, China at 41.7% and Mexico at 41.2% as moderate; and Ecuador at 39.6%, Gabon at 38.2% and Malaysia at 29.7% as a significant downturn. So the spread runs from clear expansion in Brazil to a severe downturn in Malaysia, with most of the sample between 38% and 50% and only Malaysia far below. The reporting gives no prior-period readings, so whether these represent deterioration or recovery from worse levels is not visible here. It does not give the survey's coverage, sample size or the period it refers to, does not break the readings into orders, output and inventories as a conventional index would, and offers no explanation for why Brazil and Congo diverge from the rest.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Tropical timber production is upstream of panel, furniture and construction-joinery manufacture, which is where wood adhesives are consumed. A diffusion index of this kind measures the breadth of movement rather than its size, so eight of ten countries below 50% describes how widely the weakness is spread and not how deep it runs. The two divergent readings are the more informative part: Brazil expanding while Malaysia sits near 30% shows the weakness is uneven by origin. The index does not measure volumes, so it cannot show whether supply is moving between those origins, but geography is what determines which panel producers, in which regions, would see input costs move. The China reading at 41.7% is worth noting separately given the size of its panel industry. Points that may be worth considering include whether panel customers are re-sourcing between these origins, how the index has moved over prior quarters, and which regional panel markets track which of these producers.

ITTO

item.title: A McKinsey Global Institute report concludes the Strait of Hormuz crisis produced the most severe shock to energy supplies in decades, while warning that the buffers which have so far absorbed much of it are thinning.
item.description:
The report, produced with McKinsey's global energy and materials practice, identifies four absorbers: strategic reserves, alternative pipeline routes, reorganisation of trade flows, and falling demand. Its argument is that resilience so far has been drawn from stocks and substitutions that are finite, so a prolonged crisis could reduce their effectiveness. La Repubblica's account does not quantify any of this. It gives no figure for how far strategic reserves have been drawn down, no volume for the rerouted flows, no measure of the demand decline, and no threshold at which the institute considers the buffers exhausted. Nor does it give a date range for the crisis it is assessing or say how the report defines a prolonged one. The report is an assessment by a consultancy rather than a measurement of supply, and the summary available here is a secondary account of it.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The distinction the report draws is the useful one: a system that holds through a shock because it is robust and a system that holds because it is spending reserves look identical from outside while the reserves last. Energy and freight are the input lines where that difference shows up, and both feed chemical production cost and distribution cost directly. Buffers described as thinning imply that a second disruption would price differently from the first, which is a different planning question from whether the first is over. The absence of any quantification limits how far the finding can be used; it establishes a direction, not a level. Points that may be worth considering include which of the four absorbers matters most for European supply specifically, whether current energy contracts assume a return to pre-crisis routing, and what the full report quantifies that this summary does not.

La Repubblica

item.title: Singapore's Beverage Container Return Scheme has collected more than 33 million drink containers, with 553 tonnes of material processed at a sorting facility in Tuas, ahead of the scheme's full rollout on 1 October.
item.description:
The operator, BCRS Ltd, unveiled the centralised Tuas facility and gave the figures as accurate to 13 September. Of the material collected, around 55% was plastic and 45% metal. Containers are returned through reverse vending machines. The reporting does not describe the scheme's incentive mechanism, the number of machines deployed, the return rate as a share of containers sold, or the target the scheme is working toward, so whether 33 million represents a strong or a weak start cannot be judged from this. It does not say what happens to the sorted material downstream, which recyclers take it, or whether the recovered plastic is destined for food-contact or lower-grade applications. It also does not state what obligations fall on beverage producers or importers when the full rollout takes effect.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A deposit return scheme is a market-access instrument as much as a recycling one, because it reaches back into how a container is built. Collection schemes of this kind raise questions about how label, liner and ink systems behave at the sorting stage, and about detachability at the recycler; the reporting does not say what the Tuas facility's process requires. The 55/45 plastic-to-metal split indicates both streams are in scope, and the two have different design consequences. Singapore is a small market, but schemes of this kind travel: the design rules a converter adopts for one tend to become the default across a region. Points that may be worth considering include what the scheme's sorting process requires of label and closure systems, whether customers in the region are already reformulating for it, and what the full rollout requires of producers from 1 October.

Channel News Asia

item.title: Wang Du of the China Automobile Dealers Association said the industry's average new-car gross margin has fallen to minus 21.4%, and that the domestic passenger car market may see double-digit negative growth this year.
item.description:
A negative gross margin means new-car sales are not covering their own cost at the point of sale; the reporting does not say what offsets it. Wang set out three changes he sees driving it: electrification and intelligence reshaping vehicles, mobility and the distribution system; competition reaching what he called a knockout phase; and the industry's centre of gravity moving from front-end manufacturing to the aftermarket and the existing vehicle parc. He put national vehicle ownership at 371 million, heading for 450 million. The reporting does not give the period over which the margin figure is measured, does not say whether it covers all brands or a dealer association sample, and does not compare it with any prior year, so the rate of deterioration is not visible. It also does not separate domestic brands from international ones, and the sales statement is one official's projection, hedged with "may", rather than a recorded outcome.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A distribution channel operating below cost transmits pressure upstream rather than absorbing it, and it does so through specification as much as through price. When the profit pool moves to the aftermarket and the existing parc, the volume that matters shifts from vehicles built to vehicles maintained, which is a different material mix: repair and refinish consumption rather than assembly consumption. The inventory figure is the nearer-term signal, because stock above two months at the dealer end usually precedes production adjustment at the manufacturer end. The parc numbers point the other way over a longer horizon, toward a large and growing installed base. Points that may be worth considering include how exposure splits between assembly and aftermarket demand in China, what a knockout phase among domestic brands does to supplier qualification, and whether the margin figure has a comparable in earlier years.

China Economic Net

item.title: Scott Bessent and Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on 20 September and agreed to establish an AI dialogue mechanism, but reached no agreement on extending the trade truce agreed at Busan, which expires in November.
item.description:
The Financial Times reports the AI mechanism as a step to reduce risks from the technology, and Commercial Times describes it as including a notification system for incidents that rise to national-security level. On the truce, Greer said on 21 September that there is still time to settle terms. The gap is about duration rather than principle: Commercial Times, attributing the detail to the Financial Times, reports that the US proposed a six-month extension while China wanted an extension running to the end of Trump's term. POLITICO reports that Trump and Xi are expected to extend the truce and that other deliverables will be more modest, covering agricultural trade and non-tariff barriers, and quotes Greer as saying earlier in September that the two sides are looking to manage the relationship rather than strike a comprehensive deal. So an expectation about the leaders sits alongside the negotiators' failure to agree. On the expiry date the sources differ: Commercial Times gives 10 November 2026, while the Financial Times and POLITICO say only November. The reporting does not say what happens to tariff rates if that date passes without an extension, and does not connect the AI mechanism to the trade track.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The truce is the instrument holding the tariff schedule between the world's two largest goods economies in place, and an expiry date without an agreed extension is a planning input rather than a political story. For a manufacturer with plants in both markets and customers in both, the question is not the summit's atmospherics but whether the November date moves. The disagreement over duration is informative on its own: a six-month extension and one running to the end of a presidential term describe different planning horizons, and the difference between them is roughly the lead time on a qualification or a sourcing switch. The reporting does not connect the AI mechanism to the tariff track, so on the evidence available it carries no stated tariff consequence. Points that may be worth considering include which product lines would see tariff changes if 10 November passed without an extension, whether the summit produces a duration or only an intention, and how a six-month horizon would differ from one running to the end of the presidential term.

Financial Times | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | POLITICO

item.title: IG Metall held protests against German car industry job cuts on 21 September, and a Mercedes-Benz works council deputy told the Stuttgart rally that management wants to further reduce volume at all German sites in the long term.
item.description:
The union ran the actions under the slogan "Future instead of clear-cutting", with company meetings, marches and rallies. Its first chairwoman Christiane Benner accused manufacturers of a one-sided focus on cost cuts; the district head for Berlin-Brandenburg-Saxony, Jan Otto, said at a Volkswagen engine plant in Chemnitz that managers had slept through electrification, digitalisation and battery technology and that tens of thousands of jobs had already gone. Workers from Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Bosch took part. Michael Häberle of the Mercedes group works council indicated that capacity at German sites could continue to decline. Handelsblatt separately reports that, independently of the coming collective bargaining round, Mercedes management is discussing an adjustment of working hours with its works councils, including a 38-hour week, wanting German employees to work longer for the same pay, along with concessions on Christmas and holiday bonuses and annual profit-sharing, to cut cost per working hour. MarketScreener records that Volkswagen has cut its earnings forecast after approving restructuring that could double total job losses to 100,000, and that Mercedes outlined plans last year that include shifting some production to lower-cost countries such as Hungary. The reporting gives no site-level volume figures, no timetable for the Mercedes reductions and no employer response to the union's charges beyond a call for policy reform.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Two different things are moving here and they point in opposite directions for a supplier. Job cuts reduce labour intensity without necessarily reducing vehicles built. Volume reductions at German sites reduce the vehicles themselves, and where production moves to Hungary or elsewhere the material demand moves with it rather than disappearing. The Mercedes statement is the one that bears on where material is consumed, because it describes an intention about German volume rather than about headcount; it is an intention in the long term, not a programme with a timetable. The working-time discussion is a signal of how far cost pressure has run: a 38-hour week for the same pay is a unit-cost measure of the kind that usually precedes, rather than follows, decisions about where to build. Points that may be worth considering include whether German-site volume assumptions still hold for the coming planning period, how far the relocation destinations are already served, and what the collective bargaining round in the metal and electrical industry settles on working time.

FAZ | Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | Wallstreet:online

item.title: Federal Statistical Office figures show German exports of pure electric cars to the US fell 56.1% to about 25,000 units in January to July 2026, while combustion-engine exports to the US rose 31.7% to 198,000.
item.description:
Total German new car exports fell 4.0% to just under two million units in the same period, with export value down 8.9% to EUR 73.5 billion — a steeper fall in value than in volume. The United Kingdom, the United States and Italy together took 32.7% of the total. Across all destinations the picture is flatter than the US numbers suggest: pure electric exports fell 2.9% to 560,000 units and held a near-constant 28.1% share of exported new cars, combustion exports also fell 2.9% to about one million, and hybrids fell 8.2% to 380,000. So the drivetrain reversal is not visible in the all-destination totals, and the reporting breaks out no other individual market. The reporting does not explain the reversal. It does not separate tariff effects from model availability, from demand conditions, or from manufacturers rerouting electric output to other markets, and it gives no monthly path, so whether the shift accelerated or stabilised within the seven months is not visible.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Drivetrain mix is relevant to material content rather than only to volume, because battery assembly and combustion powertrains pose different bonding, sealing and thermal-management requirements — a link the export statistics do not themselves address. On the reported bases the shift is large in units as well as in percentages: electric units to the US fell by roughly 32,000 while combustion units rose by roughly 48,000, so what crosses that route changed in composition and not only in total. Across all destinations the value decline of 8.9% runs steeper than the volume decline of 4.0%, which is a mix or price question at the aggregate level and separate from the US drivetrain pattern. Points that may be worth considering include how adhesive technologies content per vehicle differs across the two drivetrains, which the reporting does not address, whether the US pattern is appearing in other export destinations, and what the flat all-destination electric share implies about where that output went instead.

Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: A decree signed by Vladimir Putin on 21 September placed Aptar Vladimir, the Russian subsidiary of packaging group AptarGroup, under temporary government control and transferred it to an entity the report identifies only as H&N (Health & Nutrition).
item.description:
Aptar Vladimir was held through Aptar Europe Holding; AptarGroup is a packaging supplier, which is background rather than something the report states. The Moscow Times places it in a sequence that now covers at least 30 foreign companies whose Russian assets have been seized since the 2022 invasion, naming Carlsberg, Fortum, Uniper, Ariston and Bosch among them. It cites the Kyiv School of Economics Institute putting the pre-takeover value of seized foreign assets at about USD 74 billion, and total losses for companies leaving Russia at about USD 170 billion once write-offs, court rulings and exit taxes are counted. The report sets the decree against Donald Trump signing into law a sanctions bill allowing punitive tariffs on countries buying Russian oil and gas, but is explicit that it was not immediately clear whether the seizure was retaliation for that legislation. The reporting does not give the plant's capacity, product lines, headcount or revenue, does not say what H&N is or who controls it beyond the name, and does not state whether AptarGroup has any route of appeal or compensation. It also does not say whether other packaging or materials producers are under consideration.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The companies named so far in the reporting are brewers, utilities and appliance makers, though they are six examples from a list of at least thirty. A packaging-component producer would be a different kind of target, if the plant's output is components rather than consumer goods, which the reporting does not establish. For anyone still running a Russian legal entity in materials, converting or packaging, the read is that category is no longer a reason to expect to be passed over. Where packaging components are specified against a named plant, a change of control can raise a qualification question as well as a procurement one, on timescales a decree does not allow for; the reporting does not address whether that applies here. Points that may be worth considering include which suppliers of packaging components still hold Russian production, how long re-qualification of a packaging component typically runs, and whether the hedge in the reporting about retaliation resolves either way in the coming weeks.

The Moscow Times

item.title: The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers has argued against a US diesel export ban, saying refineries producing 5.3 million barrels a day of distillate against domestic demand of 3.6 million would cut runs rather than stockpile.
item.description:
The association's case is that a ban removes the outlet for the surplus rather than redirecting it, because refiners cannot hold unlimited distillate inventory and would reduce throughput instead. It names Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Energy Secretary Chris Wright as sharing that view, and quotes CIBC Private Wealth's Rebecca Babin on refiners cutting diesel production. A second argument is about credibility rather than volumes: the United States spent a decade becoming the supplier of last resort for distillate, and a ban framed as temporary tells buyers from Mexico to Germany that American supply is politically conditional, prompting them to contract elsewhere and pay for reliability. The association says a ban could increase costs for import-dependent regions such as New England, especially as heating oil demand rises. The backdrop is an oil price that ABC reported at USD 110 a barrel as the Gulf conflict spread to the Red Sea. The reporting does not say who has proposed the ban, at what stage it sits, or whether any legislative or executive vehicle exists for it. Nor does it quantify the price effect the association expects, in the US or in importing markets.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Diesel is the freight cost line that sits underneath every physical shipment, and European and Latin American buyers are among the destinations for US distillate. A ban that reduced US refinery runs would tighten a market already carrying a war premium, and the effect would reach inbound raw material movements and outbound distribution alike rather than any single plant. The second-order point is the one the association makes about contracting behaviour: buyers that re-source on reliability grounds tend to lock in term arrangements, which changes the shape of freight cost for years rather than months. Refinery run cuts also matter upstream of fuel, because the same crude units produce the naphtha and intermediate streams that feed petrochemical chains. The argument here is an industry association's, made in its own interest, and the production and demand figures are the only measurements in it. Points that may be worth considering include whether any concrete proposal exists to track, how distillate exposure sits in current freight contracts, and which European import routes would tighten first.

AFPM | AFPM | ABC
